rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem: If \(p^2 = \dfrac{32}{50}\), then p is a/an
rows.solution:
\(p^2 = \dfrac{32}{50} = \dfrac{16}{25}\), so \(p = \pm\dfrac{4}{5}\). This is a ratio of integers but not an integer.

This is option (C) rational number.

rows.subtopic: Distance Formula
rows.stem: The distance of the point \((-6, 8)\) from \(x\)-axis is
rows.solution:
The distance of a point from the x-axis is the absolute value of its y-coordinate: \(|8| = 8\). (A distance is never negative.)

This is option (C) 8 units.

rows.subtopic: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
rows.stem: The number of quadratic polynomials having zeroes \(-5\) and \(-3\) is
rows.solution:
Every polynomial \(k(x + 5)(x + 3)\) with \(k \neq 0\) is quadratic and has zeroes \(-5\) and \(-3\). There is one for each non-zero value of k, so there are infinitely many.

This is option (D) more than 3.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem: The point of intersection of the line represented by \(3x - y = 3\) and y-axis is given by
rows.solution: On the y-axis \(x = 0\), so \(3(0) - y = 3\) and \(y = -3\). The point is \((0, -3)\), which is option (A) \((0, -3)\).

rows.subtopic: Area of a Sector
rows.stem: The circumferences of two circles are in the ratio \(4 : 5\). What is the ratio of their radii ?
rows.solution:
Circumference \(= 2\pi r\), so the circumferences are in the same ratio as the radii: \(\dfrac{2\pi r_1}{2\pi r_2} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \dfrac{4}{5}\).

This is option (D) \(4 : 5\).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are the zeroes of the polynomial \(x^2 - 1\), then the value of \((\alpha + \beta)\) is
rows.solution:
\(x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1)\), so the zeroes are 1 and \(-1\), and \(\alpha + \beta = 0\). (Equivalently, the sum of the zeroes is \(-\dfrac{b}{a} = -\dfrac{0}{1} = 0\).)

This is option (D) \(0\).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Identities
rows.stem: \(\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} - \dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\), in simplified form, is :
rows.solution:
\(\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} - \dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta - 1}{\sin^2\theta} = \dfrac{-\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = -1\).

This is option (D) \(-1\).

rows.subtopic: Criteria for Similarity of Triangles
rows.stem: If \(\Delta PQR \sim \Delta ABC\); PQ = 6 cm, AB = 8 cm and the perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\) is 36 cm, then the perimeter of \(\Delta PQR\) is
rows.solution:
The perimeters of similar triangles are in the ratio of corresponding sides: \(\dfrac{\text{perimeter of } PQR}{\text{perimeter of } ABC} = \dfrac{PQ}{AB} = \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}\).

Perimeter of \(\Delta PQR = \dfrac{3}{4} \times 36 = 27\) cm, which is option (B) 27 cm.

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: If the quadratic equation \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) has two real and equal roots, then ‘c’ is equal to
rows.solution:
Real and equal roots need the discriminant to be zero: \(b^2 - 4ac = 0\), so \(c = \dfrac{b^2}{4a}\).

This is option (D) \(\dfrac{b^2}{4a}\).

rows.subtopic: Basic Proportionality Theorem
rows.stem: In the given figure, DE \(\parallel\) BC. If AD = 3 cm, AB = 7 cm and EC = 3 cm, then the length of AE is
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - triangle ABC with DE parallel to BC (D on AB, E on AC), marked AD 3 cm, AB 7 cm and EC 3 cm; the stem states every value. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
\(DE \parallel BC\), so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem \(\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AE}{AC}\), with \(AC = AE + 3\):

\(\dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{AE}{AE + 3}\), so \(3AE + 9 = 7AE\) and \(AE = \dfrac{9}{4} = 2.25\) cm.

This is option (B) 2.25 cm.

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: A bag contains 5 pink, 8 blue and 7 yellow balls. One ball is drawn at random from the bag. What is the probability of getting neither a blue nor a pink ball ?
rows.solution:
There are \(5 + 8 + 7 = 20\) balls. Neither blue nor pink means yellow, and there are 7 yellow balls.

\(P = \dfrac{7}{20}\), which is option (C) \(\dfrac{7}{20}\).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: The volume of a right circular cone whose area of the base is \(156\,\text{cm}^2\) and the vertical height is 8 cm, is
rows.solution:
Volume of a cone \(= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \text{area of base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 156 \times 8 = 416\ \text{cm}^3\).

This is option (D) \(416\,\text{cm}^3\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem: 3 chairs and 1 table cost ₹ 900; whereas 5 chairs and 3 tables cost ₹ 2,100. If the cost of 1 chair is ₹ \(x\) and the cost of 1 table is ₹ \(y\), then the situation can be represented algebraically as
rows.solution:
3 chairs and 1 table cost ₹ 900: \(3x + y = 900\).

5 chairs and 3 tables cost ₹ 2,100: \(5x + 3y = 2100\).

This is option (C) \(3x + y = 900,\; 5x + 3y = 2100\).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: In the given figure, PA and PB are tangents from external point P to a circle with centre C and Q is any point on the circle. Then the measure of \(\angle AQB\) is
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the angle of 55 degrees at P is printed only in the drawing, and only the drawing shows on which arc Q lies (opposite P, with radii CA and CB drawn). Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
The radii CA and CB are perpendicular to the tangents, so in quadrilateral PACB, \(\angle CAP = \angle CBP = 90^\circ\) and \(\angle ACB = 360^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ - 55^\circ = 125^\circ\).

In the figure Q lies on the major arc, on the side away from P. The angle subtended by arc AB at Q is half the angle it subtends at the centre: \(\angle AQB = \dfrac{125^\circ}{2} = 62\frac{1}{2}^\circ\).

This is option (A) \(62\frac{1}{2}^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: A card is drawn at random from a well shuffled deck of 52 playing cards. The probability of getting a face card is
rows.solution:
A deck has 12 face cards (a king, a queen and a jack in each of the 4 suits).

\(P(\text{face card}) = \dfrac{12}{52} = \dfrac{3}{13}\), which is option (B) \(\dfrac{3}{13}\).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Identities
rows.stem: If \(\theta\) is an acute angle of a right angled triangle, then which of the following equation is **not** true ?
rows.solution:
\(\sin\theta\cot\theta = \sin\theta \times \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \cos\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\tan\theta = \cos\theta \times \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \sin\theta\) are true, and \(\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta - \cot^2\theta = 1\) is a standard identity.

But \(\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1\), so \(\tan^2\theta - \sec^2\theta = -1\), not 1. The equation that is not true is option (D) \(\tan^2\theta - \sec^2\theta = 1\).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial \(x^2 + (a + 1)\,x + b\) are 2 and \(-3\), then
rows.solution:
For \(x^2 + (a + 1)x + b\), the sum of the zeroes is \(-(a + 1)\) and the product is b.

Sum: \(2 + (-3) = -1 = -(a + 1)\), so \(a = 0\). Product: \(2 \times (-3) = -6 = b\).

This is option (D) \(a = 0, b = -6\).

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: If the sum of the first n terms of an A.P be \(3n^2 + n\) and its common difference is 6, then its first term is
rows.solution:
The first term is the sum of the first one term: \(a = S_1 = 3(1)^2 + 1 = 4\).

(Check: \(S_2 = 14\), so the second term is \(14 - 4 = 10\), and the common difference is \(10 - 4 = 6\), as given.)

This is option (D) \(4\).

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem:
**Statement A (Assertion) :** If \(5 + \sqrt{7}\) is a root of a quadratic equation with rational co-efficients, then its other root is \(5 - \sqrt{7}\).

**Statement R (Reason) :** Surd roots of a quadratic equation with rational co-efficients occur in conjugate pairs.
rows.context: In question numbers 19 and 20, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Choose the correct option out of the following :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true; and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true; but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
If a quadratic equation has rational coefficients, its roots are \(\dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\), so an irrational (surd) root comes paired with its conjugate. The Reason is true.

By this, if \(5 + \sqrt{7}\) is a root, the other root is \(5 - \sqrt{7}\). The Assertion is true, and it follows directly from the Reason.

Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Identities
rows.stem:
**Statement A (Assertion) :** For \(0 < \theta \leq 90^\circ\), \(\operatorname{cosec}\theta - \cot\theta\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}\theta + \cot\theta\) are reciprocal of each other.

**Statement R (Reason) :** \(\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta - \cot^2\theta = 1\)
rows.context: In question numbers 19 and 20, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Choose the correct option out of the following :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true; and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true; but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
\((\operatorname{cosec}\theta - \cot\theta)(\operatorname{cosec}\theta + \cot\theta) = \operatorname{cosec}^2\theta - \cot^2\theta = 1\), so each is the reciprocal of the other. The Assertion is true.

The Reason is a standard identity, so it is true, and it is exactly what makes the product equal to 1.

Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.subtopic: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
rows.stem: Show that \(6^n\) can not end with digit 0 for any natural number ‘n’.
rows.solution:
If \(6^n\) ended with the digit 0, it would be divisible by 10, and so by 5. Then the prime factorisation of \(6^n\) would contain the prime 5.

But \(6^n = (2 \times 3)^n = 2^n \times 3^n\), and by the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic this factorisation is unique, so the only primes in it are 2 and 3. There is no 5.

So there is no natural number n for which \(6^n\) ends with the digit 0.

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Find the HCF and LCM of 72 and 120.
rows.solution:
\(72 = 2^3 \times 3^2\) and \(120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5\).

HCF \(= 2^3 \times 3 = 24\) (the lowest power of each common prime).

LCM \(= 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360\) (the highest power of each prime).

(Check: \(24 \times 360 = 8640 = 72 \times 120\).)

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: A line intersects y-axis and \(x\)-axis at point P and Q, respectively. If \(R(2, 5)\) is the mid-point of line segment PQ, then find the coordinates of P and Q.
rows.solution:
P is on the y-axis and Q on the x-axis, so let \(P = (0, y)\) and \(Q = (x, 0)\).

R(2, 5) is the mid-point of PQ: \(\dfrac{0 + x}{2} = 2\) and \(\dfrac{y + 0}{2} = 5\), so \(x = 4\) and \(y = 10\).

The points are \(P(0, 10)\) and \(Q(4, 0)\).

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: Find the length of the shadow on the ground of a pole of height 18 m when angle of elevation \(\theta\) of the sun is such that \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{6}{7}\).
rows.solution:
Let AB be the pole, with \(AB = 18\) m, and AP its shadow on the ground, with the sun's elevation \(\theta\) at P.

In right triangle APB: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{AB}{AP}\), so \(\dfrac{6}{7} = \dfrac{18}{AP}\) and \(AP = \dfrac{18 \times 7}{6} = 21\) m.

The shadow is 21 m long.

rows.subtopic: Tangent to a Circle
rows.stem:
In the given figure, PA is a tangent to the circle drawn from the external point P and PBC is the secant to the circle with BC as diameter.

If \(\angle AOC = 130^\circ\), then find the measure of \(\angle APB\), where O is the centre of the circle.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the circle with centre O and diameter BC on the line PBC, tangent PA, and the angle AOC marked 130 degrees; the stem states every fact used. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
BC is a diameter, so B, O and C lie on a straight line, and \(\angle AOB = 180^\circ - \angle AOC = 180^\circ - 130^\circ = 50^\circ\).

The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent PA, so \(\angle OAP = 90^\circ\).

In triangle AOP: \(\angle APB = 180^\circ - (50^\circ + 90^\circ) = 40^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Basic Proportionality Theorem
rows.stem: In the given figure, ABC is a triangle in which DE \(\parallel\) BC. If AD = \(x\), DB = \(x - 2\), AE = \(x + 2\) and EC = \(x - 1\), then find the value of \(x\).
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - triangle ABC with DE parallel to BC and the four segments labelled x, x - 2, x + 2 and x - 1; the stem states every value. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
In triangle ABC, \(DE \parallel BC\), so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\):

\(\dfrac{x}{x - 2} = \dfrac{x + 2}{x - 1}\), so \(x(x - 1) = (x + 2)(x - 2)\).

\(x^2 - x = x^2 - 4\), so \(x = 4\).

(Check: \(AD = 4\), \(DB = 2\), \(AE = 6\), \(EC = 3\), and \(\dfrac{4}{2} = \dfrac{6}{3}\).)

rows.subtopic: Criteria for Similarity of Triangles
rows.stem: Diagonals AC and BD of trapezium ABCD with AB \(\parallel\) DC intersect each other at point O. Show that \(\dfrac{OA}{OC} = \dfrac{OB}{OD}\).
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - trapezium ABCD (DC the shorter top side, AB the base) with diagonals meeting at O; the stem states the configuration. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
In triangles AOB and COD:

\(\angle OAB = \angle OCD\) (alternate angles, since \(AB \parallel DC\) and AC is a transversal), and \(\angle OBA = \angle ODC\) (alternate angles, with BD as the transversal).

So \(\Delta AOB \sim \Delta COD\) (AA similarity), and corresponding sides are proportional:

\(\dfrac{OA}{OC} = \dfrac{OB}{OD}\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: Find the ratio in which the line segment joining the points \(A(6, 3)\) and \(B(-2, -5)\) is divided by \(x\)-axis.
rows.solution:
Let the point \(P(x, 0)\) on the x-axis divide AB in the ratio \(k : 1\).

Its y-coordinate is \(\dfrac{k(-5) + 1(3)}{k + 1} = \dfrac{-5k + 3}{k + 1}\). Since P is on the x-axis, this is 0:

\(-5k + 3 = 0\), so \(k = \dfrac{3}{5}\).

The x-axis divides the segment in the ratio \(3 : 5\). (The point of division is \(\left(\dfrac{3(-2) + 5(6)}{8}, 0\right) = (3, 0)\).)

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Find the HCF and LCM of 26, 65 and 117, using prime factorisation.
rows.solution:
\(26 = 2 \times 13\), \(65 = 5 \times 13\), \(117 = 3^2 \times 13\).

The only prime common to all three is 13, so HCF \(= 13\).

LCM \(= 2 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 13 = 1170\).

rows.subtopic: Criteria for Similarity of Triangles
rows.stem: In the given figure, E is a point on the side CB produced of an isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC. If \(AD \perp BC\) and \(EF \perp AC\), then prove that \(\Delta ABD \sim \Delta ECF\).
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - isosceles triangle ABC with AD perpendicular to BC, CB produced to E, and EF perpendicular to AC with F on AC; the stem states the configuration. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
ABC is isosceles with \(AB = AC\), so the angles opposite these sides are equal: \(\angle ABC = \angle ACB\).

In triangles ABD and ECF:

\(\angle ADB = \angle EFC = 90^\circ\) (\(AD \perp BC\) and \(EF \perp AC\)),

\(\angle ABD = \angle ECF\) (\(\angle ABD = \angle ABC\), and \(\angle ECF = \angle ACB\) since E lies on CB produced and F on AC).

So \(\Delta ABD \sim \Delta ECF\) (AA similarity).

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: The sum of two numbers is 15. If the sum of their reciprocals is \(\dfrac{3}{10}\), find the two numbers.
rows.solution:
Let one number be x, so the other is \(15 - x\).

\(\dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{1}{15 - x} = \dfrac{3}{10}\), so \(\dfrac{15 - x + x}{x(15 - x)} = \dfrac{3}{10}\), that is \(150 = 3x(15 - x)\).

\(3x^2 - 45x + 150 = 0\), or \(x^2 - 15x + 50 = 0\), so \((x - 10)(x - 5) = 0\) and \(x = 10\) or \(x = 5\).

Either way the two numbers are 10 and 5. (Check: \(\dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{3}{10}\).)

rows.subtopic: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
rows.stem: If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are roots of the quadratic equation \(x^2 - 7x + 10 = 0\), find the quadratic equation whose roots are \(\alpha^2\) and \(\beta^2\).
rows.solution:
For \(x^2 - 7x + 10 = 0\): \(\alpha + \beta = 7\) and \(\alpha\beta = 10\).

\(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 2\alpha\beta = 49 - 20 = 29\), and \(\alpha^2\beta^2 = (\alpha\beta)^2 = 100\).

The quadratic equation with roots \(\alpha^2\) and \(\beta^2\) is \(x^2 - (\alpha^2 + \beta^2)x + \alpha^2\beta^2 = 0\), that is

\(x^2 - 29x + 100 = 0\).

(Check: the roots of \(x^2 - 7x + 10 = 0\) are 2 and 5, and \(x^2 - 29x + 100 = (x - 4)(x - 25)\).)

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Identities
rows.stem: Prove that \(\dfrac{1 + \sec A}{\sec A} = \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{1 - \cos A}\).
rows.solution:
LHS \(= \dfrac{1 + \sec A}{\sec A} = \dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{\cos A}}{\dfrac{1}{\cos A}} = \dfrac{\cos A + 1}{\cos A} \times \cos A = 1 + \cos A\)

\(= \dfrac{(1 - \cos A)(1 + \cos A)}{1 - \cos A} = \dfrac{1 - \cos^2 A}{1 - \cos A} = \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{1 - \cos A} =\) RHS.

rows.subtopic: Area of a Sector
rows.stem: In a circle of radius 21 cm, an arc subtends an angle of \(60^\circ\) at the centre. Find the area of the sector formed by the arc. Also, find the length of the arc.
rows.solution:
Area of the sector \(= \dfrac{\theta}{360^\circ} \times \pi r^2 = \dfrac{60}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21 \times 21 = 231\ \text{cm}^2\).

Length of the arc \(= \dfrac{\theta}{360^\circ} \times 2\pi r = \dfrac{60}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21 = 22\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that \(\angle PTQ = 2\angle OPQ\).
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the circle with centre O, tangents TP and TQ, chord PQ and radius OP with the angle OPQ marked; the stem states the configuration. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
Tangents drawn from an external point are equal, so \(TP = TQ\), and in triangle TPQ, \(\angle TPQ = \angle TQP\).

Let \(\angle PTQ = \theta\). Then \(\angle TPQ = \angle TQP = \dfrac{180^\circ - \theta}{2} = 90^\circ - \dfrac{\theta}{2}\).

The radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent TP, so \(\angle OPT = 90^\circ\).

\(\angle OPQ = \angle OPT - \angle TPQ = 90^\circ - \left(90^\circ - \dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\theta}{2}\).

So \(\angle PTQ = \theta = 2\angle OPQ\).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: A circle touches the side BC of a \(\Delta ABC\) at a point P and touches AB and AC when produced at Q and R respectively. Show that \(AQ = \dfrac{1}{2}\) (Perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\)).
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - triangle ABC with the circle below BC touching BC at P and AB, AC produced at Q and R; the stem states the configuration. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
Tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. So \(AQ = AR\) (from A), \(BQ = BP\) (from B) and \(CR = CP\) (from C).

\(2AQ = AQ + AR = (AB + BQ) + (AC + CR)\)

\(= AB + AC + (BP + CP) = AB + AC + BC\), since P lies on BC.

So \(AQ = \dfrac{1}{2}(AB + BC + CA) = \dfrac{1}{2}\) (Perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\)).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A solid is in the shape of a right-circular cone surmounted on a hemisphere, the radius of each of them being 7 cm and the height of the cone is equal to its diameter. Find the volume of the solid.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: the final volume is printed with the unit cm\(^2\); a volume is in cm\(^3\).]

The radius of the cone and of the hemisphere is 7 cm, and the height of the cone equals its diameter, 14 cm.

Volume of the solid \(=\) volume of the hemisphere \(+\) volume of the cone

\(= \dfrac{2}{3}\pi (7)^3 + \dfrac{1}{3}\pi (7)^2 \times 14 = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 7(14 + 14)\)

\(= \dfrac{154}{3} \times 28 = \dfrac{4312}{3}\ \text{cm}^3 \approx 1437.33\ \text{cm}^3\).

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: The ratio of the \(11^{\text{th}}\) term to the \(18^{\text{th}}\) term of an A.P. is \(2 : 3\). Find the ratio of the \(5^{\text{th}}\) term to the \(21^{\text{st}}\) term. Also, find the ratio of the sum of first 5 terms to the sum of first 21 terms.
rows.solution:
Let the first term be a and the common difference d.

\(\dfrac{a_{11}}{a_{18}} = \dfrac{a + 10d}{a + 17d} = \dfrac{2}{3}\), so \(3a + 30d = 2a + 34d\) and \(a = 4d\).

\(\dfrac{a_5}{a_{21}} = \dfrac{a + 4d}{a + 20d} = \dfrac{4d + 4d}{4d + 20d} = \dfrac{8d}{24d} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), so the ratio of the 5th term to the 21st term is \(1 : 3\).

\(\dfrac{S_5}{S_{21}} = \dfrac{\frac{5}{2}[2a + 4d]}{\frac{21}{2}[2a + 20d]} = \dfrac{5[8d + 4d]}{21[8d + 20d]} = \dfrac{5 \times 12d}{21 \times 28d} = \dfrac{5}{49}\).

The ratio of the sum of the first 5 terms to the sum of the first 21 terms is \(5 : 49\).

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: If the sum of first 6 terms of an A.P. is 36 and that of the first 16 terms is 256, find the sum of first 10 terms.

rows.subtopic: Mean of Grouped Data
rows.stem:
250 apples of a box were weighed and the distribution of masses of the apples is given in the following table :

| Mass (in grams) | 80 - 100 | 100 - 120 | 120 - 140 | 140 - 160 | 160 - 180 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of apples | 20 | 60 | 70 | \(x\) | 60 |

(i) Find the value of \(x\) and the mean mass of the apples.

(ii) Find the modal mass of the apples.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Elimination Method
rows.stem: Represent the information given above in terms of \(x\) and \(y\).
rows.context:
A coaching institute of Mathematics conducts classes in two batches I and II and fees for rich and poor children are different. In batch I, there are 20 poor and 5 rich children, whereas in batch II, there are 5 poor and 25 rich children. The total monthly collection of fees from batch I is ₹ 9000 and from batch II is ₹ 26,000. Assume that each poor child pays ₹ \(x\) per month and each rich child pays ₹ \(y\) per month.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: DECORATIVE - a photograph of a classroom full of students; every number is in the passage. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
Batch I has 20 poor and 5 rich children and collects ₹ 9000: \(20x + 5y = 9000\).

Batch II has 5 poor and 25 rich children and collects ₹ 26,000: \(5x + 25y = 26000\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Elimination Method
rows.stem: Find the monthly fee paid by a poor child.
rows.context:
A coaching institute of Mathematics conducts classes in two batches I and II and fees for rich and poor children are different. In batch I, there are 20 poor and 5 rich children, whereas in batch II, there are 5 poor and 25 rich children. The total monthly collection of fees from batch I is ₹ 9000 and from batch II is ₹ 26,000. Assume that each poor child pays ₹ \(x\) per month and each rich child pays ₹ \(y\) per month.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The fees satisfy \(20x + 5y = 9000\) and \(5x + 25y = 26000\), that is \(4x + y = 1800\) ... (1) and \(x + 5y = 5200\) ... (2)

From (1), \(y = 1800 - 4x\). Substituting in (2): \(x + 9000 - 20x = 5200\), so \(19x = 3800\) and \(x = 200\).

The monthly fee paid by a poor child is ₹ 200.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Elimination Method
rows.stem: Find the difference in the monthly fee paid by a poor child and a rich child.
rows.context:
A coaching institute of Mathematics conducts classes in two batches I and II and fees for rich and poor children are different. In batch I, there are 20 poor and 5 rich children, whereas in batch II, there are 5 poor and 25 rich children. The total monthly collection of fees from batch I is ₹ 9000 and from batch II is ₹ 26,000. Assume that each poor child pays ₹ \(x\) per month and each rich child pays ₹ \(y\) per month.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The fees satisfy \(20x + 5y = 9000\) and \(5x + 25y = 26000\), that is \(4x + y = 1800\) ... (1) and \(x + 5y = 5200\) ... (2)

From (1), \(y = 1800 - 4x\). Substituting in (2): \(x + 9000 - 20x = 5200\), so \(19x = 3800\), \(x = 200\) and \(y = 1800 - 800 = 1000\).

A poor child pays ₹ 200 and a rich child ₹ 1000, so the difference in the monthly fee is \(1000 - 200 =\) ₹ 800.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Elimination Method
rows.stem: If there are 10 poor and 20 rich children in batch II, what is the total monthly collection of fees from batch II ?
rows.context:
A coaching institute of Mathematics conducts classes in two batches I and II and fees for rich and poor children are different. In batch I, there are 20 poor and 5 rich children, whereas in batch II, there are 5 poor and 25 rich children. The total monthly collection of fees from batch I is ₹ 9000 and from batch II is ₹ 26,000. Assume that each poor child pays ₹ \(x\) per month and each rich child pays ₹ \(y\) per month.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Solving \(20x + 5y = 9000\) and \(5x + 25y = 26000\) gives \(x = 200\) and \(y = 1000\).

With 10 poor and 20 rich children, the collection is \(10x + 20y = 10(200) + 20(1000) = 2000 + 20000 =\) ₹ 22000.

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: Find the length of the wire from the point O to the top of Section B.
rows.context:
Radio towers are used for transmitting a range of communication services including radio and television. The tower will either act as an antenna itself or support one or more antennas on its structure. On a similar concept, a radio station tower was built in two Sections A and B. Tower is supported by wires from a point O.

Distance between the base of the tower and point O is 36 cm. From point O, the angle of elevation of the top of the Section B is \(30^\circ\) and the angle of elevation of the top of Section A is \(45^\circ\).

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the tower drawn as a vertical lattice with foot P, points B and A on it, O on the ground 36 cm from P, and the elevation angles 30 and 45 degrees at O; this part uses only the passage. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
Let P be the foot of the tower and B the top of Section B, so \(OP = 36\) cm and \(\angle BOP = 30^\circ\).

In right triangle OPB: \(\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{OP}{OB}\), so \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{36}{OB}\) and \(OB = \dfrac{72}{\sqrt{3}} = 24\sqrt{3}\) cm.

The wire from O to the top of Section B is \(24\sqrt{3}\) cm (about 41.57 cm) long.

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: Find the distance AB.
rows.context:
Radio towers are used for transmitting a range of communication services including radio and television. The tower will either act as an antenna itself or support one or more antennas on its structure. On a similar concept, a radio station tower was built in two Sections A and B. Tower is supported by wires from a point O.

Distance between the base of the tower and point O is 36 cm. From point O, the angle of elevation of the top of the Section B is \(30^\circ\) and the angle of elevation of the top of Section A is \(45^\circ\).

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the passage names Sections A and B but never the points A and B; only the drawing places point A at the top of Section A and point B at the top of Section B on the vertical tower. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
Let P be the foot of the tower, B the top of Section B and A the top of Section A, with \(OP = 36\) cm.

In right triangle OPB: \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{PB}{36}\), so \(PB = \dfrac{36}{\sqrt{3}} = 12\sqrt{3}\) cm.

In right triangle OPA: \(\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{AP}{36}\), so \(AP = 36\) cm.

\(AB = AP - PB = 36 - 12\sqrt{3} = 12(3 - \sqrt{3})\) cm (about 15.22 cm).

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: Find the area of \(\Delta OPB\).
rows.context:
Radio towers are used for transmitting a range of communication services including radio and television. The tower will either act as an antenna itself or support one or more antennas on its structure. On a similar concept, a radio station tower was built in two Sections A and B. Tower is supported by wires from a point O.

Distance between the base of the tower and point O is 36 cm. From point O, the angle of elevation of the top of the Section B is \(30^\circ\) and the angle of elevation of the top of Section A is \(45^\circ\).

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - P, the foot of the tower, and B, the top of Section B, are named only in the drawing; the passage never defines them. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
Let P be the foot of the tower and B the top of Section B, with \(OP = 36\) cm and \(\angle BOP = 30^\circ\).

In right triangle OPB: \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{PB}{36}\), so \(PB = \dfrac{36}{\sqrt{3}} = 12\sqrt{3}\) cm.

Area of \(\Delta OPB = \dfrac{1}{2} \times OP \times PB = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 36 \times 12\sqrt{3} = 216\sqrt{3}\ \text{cm}^2\) (about \(374.12\ \text{cm}^2\)).

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: Find the height of the Section A from the base of the tower.
rows.context:
Radio towers are used for transmitting a range of communication services including radio and television. The tower will either act as an antenna itself or support one or more antennas on its structure. On a similar concept, a radio station tower was built in two Sections A and B. Tower is supported by wires from a point O.

Distance between the base of the tower and point O is 36 cm. From point O, the angle of elevation of the top of the Section B is \(30^\circ\) and the angle of elevation of the top of Section A is \(45^\circ\).

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the tower drawing; this part uses only the passage. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
Let P be the foot of the tower and A the top of Section A. In right triangle OPA, \(\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{AP}{OP} = 1\), so \(AP = OP = 36\) cm.

The top of Section A is 36 cm above the base of the tower.

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: What is the probability that the drawn ball bears number 8 ?
rows.context:
“Eight Ball” is a game played on a pool table with 15 balls numbered 1 to 15 and a “cue ball” that is solid and white. Of the 15 numbered balls, eight are solid (non-white) coloured and numbered 1 to 8 and seven are striped balls numbered 9 to 15.

The 15 numbered pool balls (no cue ball) are placed in a large bowl and mixed, then one ball is drawn out at random.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: DECORATIVE - a photograph of pool balls and a cue on a table; every fact is in the passage. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
There are 15 equally likely balls, and exactly one of them bears the number 8.

\(P(\text{number } 8) = \dfrac{1}{15}\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: What is the probability that the drawn ball bears an even number ?
rows.context:
“Eight Ball” is a game played on a pool table with 15 balls numbered 1 to 15 and a “cue ball” that is solid and white. Of the 15 numbered balls, eight are solid (non-white) coloured and numbered 1 to 8 and seven are striped balls numbered 9 to 15.

The 15 numbered pool balls (no cue ball) are placed in a large bowl and mixed, then one ball is drawn out at random.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The balls bearing even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14: 7 of the 15.

\(P(\text{even number}) = \dfrac{7}{15}\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: What is the probability that the drawn ball bears a number, which is a multiple of 3 ?
rows.context:
“Eight Ball” is a game played on a pool table with 15 balls numbered 1 to 15 and a “cue ball” that is solid and white. Of the 15 numbered balls, eight are solid (non-white) coloured and numbered 1 to 8 and seven are striped balls numbered 9 to 15.

The 15 numbered pool balls (no cue ball) are placed in a large bowl and mixed, then one ball is drawn out at random.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The multiples of 3 from 1 to 15 are 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15: 5 of the 15 balls.

\(P(\text{multiple of } 3) = \dfrac{5}{15} = \dfrac{1}{3}\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: What is the probability that the drawn ball is a solid coloured and bears an even number ?
rows.context:
“Eight Ball” is a game played on a pool table with 15 balls numbered 1 to 15 and a “cue ball” that is solid and white. Of the 15 numbered balls, eight are solid (non-white) coloured and numbered 1 to 8 and seven are striped balls numbered 9 to 15.

The 15 numbered pool balls (no cue ball) are placed in a large bowl and mixed, then one ball is drawn out at random.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The solid coloured balls are numbered 1 to 8, and of these 2, 4, 6 and 8 are even: 4 of the 15 balls.

\(P(\text{solid coloured and even}) = \dfrac{4}{15}\).
